C or c

Displays numeric values in currency format. You can specify the number of decimal places. Example:

Format: {0:C} 123.456 -> $123.46

D or d

Displays integer values in decimal format. You can specify the number of digits. (Although the type is referred to as "decimal", the numbers are formatted as integers.) Example: Format: {0:D} 1234 -> 1234 Format: {0:D6} 1234 -> 001234

E or e Displays numeric values in scientific (exponential) format. You can specify the number of decimal places. Example: Format: {0:E} 1052.0329112756 -> 1.052033E+003 Format: {0:E2} -1052.0329112756 -> -1.05e+003

F or f Displays numeric values in fixed format. You can specify the number of decimal places. Example: Format: {0:F} 1234.567 -> 1234.57 Format: {0:F3} 1234.567 -> 1234.567

G or g Displays numeric values in general format (the most compact of either fixed-point or scientific notation). You can specify the number of significant digits. Example: Format: {0:G} -123.456 -> -123.456 Format: {0:G2} -123.456 -> -120

F or f Displays numeric values in fixed format. You can specify the number of decimal places. Format: {0:F} 1234.567 -> 1234.57 Format: {0:F3} 1234.567 -> 1234.567

G or g Displays numeric values in general format (the most compact of either fixed-point or scientific notation). You can specify the number of significant digits. Format: {0:G} -123.456 -> -123.456 Format: {0:G2} -123.456 -> -120

N or n Displays numeric values in number format (including group separators and optional negative sign). You can specify the number of decimal places. Format: {0:N} 1234.567 -> 1,234.57 Format: {0:N4} 1234.567 -> 1,234.5670

P or p Displays numeric values in percent format. You can specify the number of decimal places. Format: {0:P} 1 -> 100.00% Format: {0:P1} .5 -> 50.0%

R or r Displays Single, Double, or BigInteger values in round-trip format. Format: {0:R} 123456789.12345678 -> 123456789.12345678

X or x Displays integer values in hexadecimal format. You can specify the number of digits. Format: {0:X} 255 -> FF Format: {0:x4} 255 -> 00ff

Q: the best way to detect browser in js A:

These days testing for a browser environment is as simple as testing the truthiness of document.all:

// Evaluates to true in modern web browsers including IE
typeof document=='object' && !Object(document && document.all) || /*@cc_on!@*/false

In the above Object() either returns a truthy object since all objects are truthy, or limited to browsers, Object() returns a falsy document.all as per the HTML5 spec.

It all started in the ES3/HTML4 days when popular browsers wanted to support document.all without triggering IE-specific code and were already putting such measures into place. It was soon written into the HTML5 spec and is long since supported in every modern browser including Internet Explorer 11.

The || /*@cc_on!@*/false tacked on at the end is an IE-only feature and is needed to make it work in IE 10 and below.

See: Why is document.all falsy?

Q: Can you declare a property private within an abstract class? A:

Yes, you can have a private property within an abstract class. This property will only be accessible to functions within that abstract class though. Any classes which inherit from your abstract class will not be able to access the property.

You can declare both properties and methods as public, protected or private within an abstract class. If a property or method is public, it is accessible to anyone. If it is protected, it is accessible only to that class, and any classes which inherit from that class. If it is private, it is only accessible to that class.

Abstract methods must be implemented by an inheriting class, so it makes no sense (and probably won't work) to have a private abstract method.
